newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine optimistic about treaty with Romania.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine optimistic about treaty with Romania.

text.p: Ukraine's top negotiator in talks with Romania expressed optimism on Tuesday that a long delayed post-communist treaty, vital for Bucharest's chances of early entry to NATO, would be clinched this week.

First Deputy Foreign Minister Anton Buteiko, speaking after the arrival of a Romanian delegation, pledged Ukraine would be flexible. He suggested both sides put off discussions on borders on the Black Sea shelf and possible oil and gas rights.

"Ukraine has been ready for a treaty with Romania for a long time. We are ready for compromise," Buteiko told reporters. "We do not think this (economic zone and shelf) is a specific problem. Right after the treaty is signed Ukraine will be ready to start defining this line."
Romania's new centrist leadership, which sees rapid NATO membership as its chief foreign policy goal, has also signalled it is willing to make compromises to secure a deal with Kiev.

Western leaders have praised Romania's conclusion last year of a treaty with Hungary and say its bid to beat the odds and win quick admission to NATO alongside favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic depends on a similar accord with Ukraine.

Unlike Russia, Ukraine says it has no objections to NATO expansion and has even hinted it might one day be able to join the Alliance itself. Moldova, sandwiched between Ukraine and Romania, also offers no opposition to an expanded NATO.
The talks, in their ninth round, have stalled on Romanian insistence that Ukraine atone for the Kremlin's 1940 seizure of chunks of Romanian territory under the Nazi-Soviet pact.

But Romanian officials this week said their main concern had shifted to setting down Black Sea borders. Ukraine wants an unequivocal statement that neither side will make territorial claims against the other.
Romanian President Emil Constantinescu, who ousted an ex-communist in last year's election, has said his country is ready to make "historic sacrifices".

"We are ready to recognise (current) borders," he told Ukraine's private Nova Mova television channel before the talks got under way. "This recognition of reality will effectively form the basis of a treaty."
Constantinescu also acknowledged that Serpent Island, a rocky outcrop off both countries' Black Sea coasts, was Ukrainian territory.
Several hundred Ukrainian troops maintain a rotating presence on the island, which Romania says was unfairly ceded to the Soviet Union by Romanian communists in the 1950s.

Both sides are keenly aware of potential offshore oil and gas deposits around the island. Ukrainian officials estimate that up to 7,000 square km (2,800 square miles) of Black Sea territory may be in dispute.

Buteiko also said Ukrainian negotiators would seek improved rights, including more schools, for what they say may be up to 300,000 ethnic Ukrainians in Romania. About 200,000 ethnic Romanians live in post-Soviet Ukraine.
